title: "Importing from an older atima"

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE)
```

This article is for the administrator of a site that ran atima 2, the
Shiny application with a MariaDB or MySQL database, and wants its users'
projects on a current atima. It describes the three things the
administrator does, what each person then does, what comes over and what
does not, and what to watch for while people move. Other old versions of
atima cannot be imported from.

**A person who has forgotten their old password cannot import their
projects, and nobody else can do it for them.** atima 2 encrypted every
project with keys that only its users' passwords unlock. The administrator
does not have those keys, and the old database does not contain them in a
form anyone can use without the password.


## How it works

Because of that encryption, an administrator cannot move the data alone.
Instead:

1. The administrator saves the old database to one file, once.
2. The administrator tells the new server where the file is.
3. Each person signs in to the new server, types the email address and
   password they had on the old site, and chooses which projects to bring
   over. The server checks the password against the file and decrypts that
   person's projects in memory.

The old database server is only needed for step 1.


## Step 1: save the old database

Do this on a computer that can reach the old database, with the `atima`
and `RMariaDB` packages installed. A database account that may only
`SELECT` is enough. The old database is read and not changed.

```{r}
con <- DBI::dbConnect(
  RMariaDB::MariaDB(),
  dbname   = "atima",
  host     = "<database host>",
  user     = "<user>",
  password = Sys.getenv("ATIMA2_DB_PASSWORD") )

atima::legacy_convert(con, "atima2.sqlite")
DBI::dbDisconnect(con)
```

`legacy_convert()` reports how many accounts, projects and objects it
copied. The file it names must not exist yet. Converting a database with
about 5,000 projects took less than a minute and gave a file of a little
under 1 GB.

If all you have is a `mysqldump` file, restore it into any MariaDB server
first and connect to that. The tables needed are `Users`, `Projects`,
`Permissions` and `Objects`.

### What is in the file

| In the file | Not in the file |
|-------------|-----------------|
| For each account with an email address: the email address, the bcrypt hash of the password, and the account's encrypted private key. | Names and affiliations. |
| For each project that was not deleted: who could open it and at what level, and its BIOM file, metadata, taxonomy, tree, name and rarefaction depth, each still encrypted as atima 2 stored it. | Sessions, sign-in tokens and cached results. |
| | Who could view the old site's public example projects, since every account could. |

Nothing is decrypted by the conversion. The file is as sensitive as the
old database was: it holds password hashes and email addresses. Keep it
out of version control and readable only by the account the server runs
as.


## Step 2: register the file

Install the `bcrypt` package where the server runs:

```{r}
install.packages("bcrypt")
```

Then name the file when starting the server, with the label people should
see for it:

```{r}
atima::run(
  auth   = "oidc",
  legacy = c("ATIMA 2 (2019 to 2026)" = "/srv/atima/atima2.sqlite") )
```

or with an environment variable, `<label>=<file>`:

```sh
ATIMA_LEGACY="ATIMA 2 (2019 to 2026)=/srv/atima/atima2.sqlite"
```

Several installations are separated by `;`. A label may have at most 60
characters.

The server only reads the file. It refuses to start if the file is
missing, was not made by `legacy_convert()`, or if `bcrypt` is not
installed, and says which.

When the server runs in a container, mount the file read-only. The article
[Running a shared server](server.html) shows how.

### Give the server at least two workers

An import runs in a worker process, one project at a time per person, and
one large project may hold that worker for up to 15 minutes. With
`workers = 1`, everyone's figures wait behind it. Start a server that
people import to with `workers = 2` or more.


## Step 3: what each person does

Someone who has signed in finds **Import from an older atima** in the
menu. (A guest is asked to sign in first. On a local atima,
`auth = "none"`, the link is there for the local user.) They:

1. Enter the email address and password they used on the old site, and
   choose "Find my projects".
2. Tick the projects to bring over, and choose "Import selected".
3. Keep working, or close the page. The import runs on the server in the
   background, and a notice says when it is done.

Tell your users the following.

**How long it takes.** Most projects take a few seconds. A project with
tens of thousands of taxa can take several minutes. One project may take
at most 15 minutes; a larger one is reported as not imported.

**The import can be interrupted.** A person can cancel their import. A
restart of the server ends running imports. In both cases, what was
imported stays, and the rest can be started again with the same steps.

**Counts that are not whole numbers.** Such a project is listed as "Not
imported: its counts are not whole numbers". The person can choose "Scale
and import" after typing the old password again; atima then scales the
counts to whole numbers once, as it does for an upload.

**Five wrong passwords.** After five wrong passwords in 15 minutes, the
person must wait, and so must anyone else who tries that old account.

**One import at a time.** A person has one import running at a time.


## What comes over

| Comes over | Does not come over |
|------------|--------------------|
| Samples, counts, metadata, taxonomy and tree, as the project last had them on the old site, including edits made there. | The old account itself. The person's name on the new server comes from the sign-in provider. |
| The project's name, creation date and rarefaction depth. | Sessions and cached results. |
| Sharing, as people arrive (see below). | The old site's public example projects, except for people who could edit them. |
| | Projects that were deleted on the old site. |

### How sharing carries over

A project is imported once. The first person to import it brings it over.
When someone else who could open it on the old site imports it later, they
are added to that same project instead of getting a copy.

Everyone gets the access they had on the old site, editor or viewer, and
never more. Someone who could only view a project can only view it on the
new server. If a viewer is the first to import a project, the project has
no editor until one of its old editors imports it. Until then the viewer
can use "Save a copy" to get a project of their own that they can change.

Importing a project again does not duplicate it: the list shows it as
"Already in your projects".


## What the server does with the old password

- The password is sent to the server over the same connection as
  everything else, which is why a shared server must use HTTPS.
- It is checked, and the projects are decrypted, in memory in a worker
  process.
- The server keeps the password in memory while that person's import
  runs, and drops it when the last project is done.
- The password and the keys it unlocks are never written to the database,
  the log or a file.
- Wrong attempts are counted in the database, so a restart does not reset
  the count. The old email address is kept there only as a hash. These
  rows are removed after a day, the next time anyone makes an attempt.


## What to watch for in the server log

The server log is one line of JSON per event. Search it for:

| In the log | Meaning | What to do |
|------------|---------|------------|
| `legacy_import_failed` | A project could not be imported for a reason the person cannot do anything about. They see "Not imported" with an error id; the log line has the same `id`, the old project's id (`old_project`) and the reason (`message`). | If the message says the project took longer than the 900 seconds allowed, the project is too large for the 15 minute limit. Otherwise report it at <https://github.com/cmmr/atima/issues> with the log line, after checking that it holds nothing private. The person's other projects are not affected. |
| `encryption key could not be rebuilt` | The person's password was right, but atima could not rebuild the key that atima 2 derived from it. atima 2 derived this key in a way that depended on the old server's software, and atima tries the variants that are known. The line names the old user id. | Report it. That person cannot import until atima knows the variant their account used. |
| `legacy_start`, `legacy_import`, `legacy_done` | An import started, a project arrived, an import finished. | Nothing. They show how the move is going. |
| An `error` line with status 429 and "Too many wrong passwords" | Someone is locked out for up to 15 minutes. | Nothing, unless one address does it many times: see below. |

Each password check costs a worker about a second of work. A person is
stopped after five wrong passwords, but a script could try many accounts.
If the server is public, have the reverse proxy limit how often one
address may call the paths under `/api/legacy/`; see
[Running a shared server](server.html).

Imports count towards `jobs_per_user`, and wait their turn in the same
queue as figures. When the queue is full, an import waits and tries again
every five seconds.


## Limits

| Limit | Value |
|-------|-------|
| Time for one project | 15 minutes |
| Imports per person at a time | 1 |
| Projects in one import | 2,000 |
| Wrong passwords | 5 in 15 minutes, per person and per old account |
| Supported old version | atima 2 only |


## When everyone has moved

Remove the `legacy` setting, restart the server, and delete the file and
every copy of it. People who have not imported by then cannot do so
afterwards, so announce a date first. If you keep the file for stragglers,
keep it as carefully as the old database.
